To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cumulative positivity rate of enteric pathogens was 6.1%, and the positivity rate for 1,923 samples obtained from patients hospitalized < or = 7 days was 11.5%, while it dropped to 2.2% for samples obtained from patients with longer hospital stays (P < 0001).

the use of stool cultures for enteric bacteria should be limited to patients with acute diarrhea and no antimicrobial treatment, and that the testing for cytotoxins should be restricted to patients under antimicrobial agents.
the positivity rate of bacterial cultures decreases when patients receive antimicrobial agents and that the positivity rate decreases further with the duration of hospitalization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of stool cultures in the clinical microbiology practice and with the impact that the results of these tests have on the management of patients.
the use of microbial cultures for the diagnosis of infectious diarrhea.
the rationalization of the use of diagnostic tests, which are expensive and often unnecessary.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the majority of patients do not need to be cultured for enteric bacteria and that, when a patient does need to be cultured, a single sample should be requested.
the majority of stool specimens do not need to be submitted for bacterial culture.
the request for bacterial culture for patients hospitalized for more than 3 days should be avoided.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of stool cultures for enteric bacteria are unnecessary, and that they should be restricted to the above-mentioned patient populations.

the use of culture for enteric bacterial agents in our hospital should be restricted to patients under antimicrobial agents, patients with diarrhea lasting < or = 72 h, or patients with a first culture negative result.

the use of culture for enteric bacterial agents should be restricted to the first 3 days of the hospitalization of the patient, with the exception of immunocompromised individuals and patients whose first samples were culture negative.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the absence of clinical indications, the use of cultures is not justified for the majority of patients.
the use of culture for enteric pathogens should be restricted to patients who are hospitalized for < or > 3 days.
the use of stool cultures for the diagnosis of enteric pathogens is limited.
